notes: Flat tax: 4.25% for 2025 (PDF page 3; page 10 Line 17). Married filing separately, head of household and qualifying surviving spouse have no own schedule: head of household and qualifying surviving spouse must file Michigan as single (page 10 Line 7).

Michigan retirement rules are by birth year of the older spouse (key person); each birth-year branch is its own relief entry, and all retirement subtractions plus Tier 2/Tier 3 Michigan Standard Deductions share best_of_group mi_retirement_choice because the booklet says a recipient born before 1967 may qualify for several options but may claim only one.

Born after December 31, 1966: booklet says they do not qualify for a retirement and pension subtraction unless allowed under another section (the SSA-exempt retired-by-2013 entry; surviving spouse exceptions); all benefits in AGI are taxable. Not a relief entry because there is nothing to subtract.

Date discrepancy: the heading for SSA-exempt recipients says born January 1, 1959 through January 1, 1964, but Line 18 says January 2, 1959 through January 1, 1964; I used 1959-01-02 (Line 18). Likewise SSA-exempt retired-by-2013 heading says 'born after January 1, 1959' and I used 1959-01-02. Born January 1, 1959 falls in the Tier 3 / Section D branch.

Caps of 49,423 / 98,846 are printed as such on Line 19 and the pages; Worksheet 3.3 computes 75% of 65,897 / 131,794 less military, National Guard and railroad retirement (75% of 65,897 = 49,422.75, printed rounded to 49,423).

Public vs private: pre-1946 and fire/police entries are split into a public entry (no cap) and a private entry (cap 65,897 / 131,794). For the 1946-1966 and SSA-exempt branches the cap is on total public and private benefits, so there is one entry each; worksheets 3.1 and 3.2 count public benefits first and cap private benefits at the remaining room.

Fire/police: the booklet says the recipient may claim the most beneficial of option (a) (public all, private to 65,897/131,794) or a Michigan Standard Deduction by year of birth, so the two entries share the group; the surviving spouse of a fire/police retiree also qualifies.

Qualifying surviving spouse (claimed a retirement or Social Security subtraction on the joint return in the year of death and not remarried; spouse died before 2025) uses the older of self or deceased spouse's birth year; recorded in other_conditions and here only, not as its own entries.

roth_conversion: the booklet never mentions Roth conversions; it says IRA distributions after age 59 1/2 (or a series of equal periodic payments for life under IRC 72(t)(2)(A)(iv)) qualify, so roth_conversion is in covers_unclear. Qualifying annuity: retirement annuity policy paid to a senior citizen (65 or older) for life. Foreign plans meeting Michigan's qualifications may be eligible.

Standard deduction 'covers': the booklet says it applies 'against all income types', so every income kind except social_security and military/railroad (which reduce the amount) is listed; Social Security is instead subtracted separately (Tier 3 reduces it by taxable Social Security).

Social Security treated as exempt: Schedule 1 line 14 subtracts the taxable portion of Social Security included in AGI (page 14); no explicit sentence says 'Michigan does not tax Social Security'. Tier 1 and Tier 2 railroad retirement is subtracted on line 11.

Municipal interest: Schedule 1 line 1 adds back interest and dividends from obligations of states and political subdivisions other than Michigan; the booklet does not say outright that Michigan's own obligations are exempt, so own-state exemption is inferred from the 'other than Michigan' wording. U.S. government obligation interest is subtracted (line 10).

Capital gains: no separate rate or deduction share is printed; gains are taxed as other income except the age-based line 28 deduction and Michigan adjustments (MI-1040D) for pre-1967 property, U.S. obligations and out-of-state property. capital_gains is empty.

Exemption: 5,800 per exemption claimed (self, spouse, each dependent) plus stillbirth exemption of 5,800 (line 9d); special exemption 3,400 for deaf, blind, hemiplegic, paraplegic, quadriplegic or totally and permanently disabled (one per person, not for someone who reached 66 by Feb 28, 2025 as totally and permanently disabled); 500 for a qualified disabled veteran; 1,500 on line 9e if someone else can claim you (with 0 on line 9a). The special exemption is recorded with what 'other' since the schema has no combined deaf/blind/disabled value.

Left out: Renaissance Zone subtraction, tribal member subtraction, 529/MET deductions, severance-tax and marihuana items, federal elderly/disabled credit subtraction (line 23, only as a reducer), P.A. 24 of 2025 IRC decoupling adjustments, credits (EITC 30% of federal, out-of-state tax credit, homestead property tax credit), and all non-retirement subtractions.
Indexing: the booklet does not say any figure is adjusted for inflation; it gives 2025-specific amounts. Recorded as not_stated for all figures.

Schema limits: no field for 'smaller of public/private rules interacting' beyond cap_rule text; reductions by military, railroad, taxable Social Security, exemptions and active-duty pay are in cap_rule text only; per-spouse doubling for SSA-exempt entries (30,000 / 70,000) is in cap_rule only.

Settlement 2026-11-06: reading A taken as the record; reading B merged public and private benefits for births before 1946 under one capped entry, which the booklet does not support (public benefits are not capped).
Format update 2026-11-06: recapture added (none found in the booklet).

2026-11-07 (from the hand-worked checks): Worksheet 3.3 cites corrected to PDF page 25; projection: pre-1946 public and private subtractions stack (not a best-of group), another state's government pension counts as private, Tier 2/3 bounded by birth date only, the 75% cap reduction recorded as an approximation.
